subject: english-literature
title: Jealousy, Race and the Cinthio Source
welcome_lead: Open Shakespeare's 1603 tragedy and trace how he transforms Cinthio's Italian novella into a meditation on race, jealousy and trust.
meta_desc: A-Level OCR adventure on Shakespeare's Othello (1603): jealousy, race, Iago, and the Cinthio source.
final_note: Shakespeare gives the Moor a tragic interior Cinthio never imagined. The play insists Othello is great — which is what makes Iago's destruction so total.

concepts.def: Giraldi Cinthio's 1565 Italian novella collection; the seventh story of the third decade provides Shakespeare's plot — 'Disdemona' and an unnamed 'Moor'.
Aristotelian protagonist of stature whose hamartia precipitates downfall; Othello's stature is racially marked, his fall amplified.
Iago calls it 'the green-eyed monster'; the play anatomises jealousy as epistemic rather than purely emotional — a way of misreading the world.
The play's longest part (more lines than Othello); a Vice-figure descendant who weaponises his audience access through soliloquy.
Othello is repeatedly called 'Moor', 'thick-lips', 'the Barbary horse' — Shakespeare stages early modern racial categories with critical sharpness.
The play borrows from the emerging genre of bourgeois domestic tragedy (Arden of Faversham, A Woman Killed with Kindness) by locating tragedy in marriage.

walkthroughs.body_html: Cinthio's 1565 novella 'Un Capitano Moro' features a Moorish captain, his Venetian wife Disdemona, and a malevolent ensign. Shakespeare names his villain Iago (Spanish form of James, the patron saint who reputedly slew Moors at Clavijo), gives Othello a name and a tragic stature, and compresses the action. Crucially, Shakespeare invents Othello's eloquence — Cinthio's Moor is largely silent. The 'Othello music' (G. Wilson Knight, 1930) is Shakespeare's addition.

Othello was likely performed at the Banqueting House at Whitehall on 1 November 1604 (Hallowmas) — a documented court performance. Composition probably dates 1603. James I had just acceded, and English diplomatic contact with Morocco was active (the Moroccan ambassador had visited London in 1600). Critics including Emily Bartels (Speaking of the Moor, 2008) argue Shakespeare's audience had complex, not uniformly negative, conceptions of 'Moors'.

Until the late 20th century, critics including A.C. Bradley downplayed race; Bradley argued Othello is a 'noble Moor' whose colour is incidental. More recent critics — Kim F. Hall, Ania Loomba, Joyce Green MacDonald — insist race is structural to the play's tragic logic. Iago's racial slurs at 1.1 ('an old black ram', 'the Barbary horse') are not incidental but constitutive: they prefigure the colonial discourse Othello internalises.
